title: Prelude: divides operator ∣ (U+2223) and not-divides ∤ (U+2224)
description:
OWNER DECISION 2026-11-12 (spec confirmed by the owner; implement exactly, then two independent rig-reviews + api-review label, agent-merge per decision 1):

- (n ∣ m): m % n = 0. True when n divides m. Mathematical order: 3 ∣ 12 is true, 12 ∣ 3 is false. Pipeline use: xs filter(3 ∣ _) keeps multiples of 3.
- (n ∤ m): not(n ∣ m), mirroring ∉ / ∈.
- Metadata: associates :left, precedence :eq (the same as =), so a + b ∣ c * d is (a + b) ∣ (c * d), and ∧/∨ combine results.
- Defined in lib/prelude.eu in terms of %. No new intrinsic. A zero divisor and non-integers behave exactly as % does (inherit its errors).
- Doc metadata on both (backtick markdown). Docs: operators reference, cheat sheet (docs/appendices/cheat-sheet.md), agent-reference, regenerated prelude reference pages. Note in the docs that ∣ (U+2223) is not | (bitwise or).

Verify the parser/lexer accepts U+2223 and U+2224 as operator characters; if it doesn't, that's a frontend fix in the same PR.
- Editor grammars: note the two operators on eu-ioz21 for the grammar lanes.

title: Compile strict arguments call-by-value (evaluate in place) instead of thunk-then-seq
description: From eu-oaz72.27 (PR #1158, docs/superpowers/reports/2026-11-12-strict-accumulators.md). When demand analysis proves an argument strict, the compiler still allocates a thunk and then forces it (let x = thunk in seq x in f(x)). That costs about +3 ticks per iteration on strict accumulator loops (loop A at n=1e6: 37.0M to 40.0M ticks after #1158) and is the main obstacle to a foldl-strict that is cheaper than foldl. Compile a proven-strict argument by evaluating it in place, with no thunk. This is a compiler change only, with no new API; semantics are unchanged because strictness is proven. Starts after #1158 merges. eucalypt-backend and eucalypt-performance skills; any tick claim follows the measurement protocol.

Restricted to that set because a case continuation strips metadata whereas thunk+Update memoises a Meta value; these primops never return a Meta, so the value passed is identical. title: (BUG) Intrinsics report the machine's stale annotation after forcing their arguments, so errors point at the last annotated code evaluated
description: From eu-oaz72.32 (PR #1155). An intrinsic reads the machine's current annotation after its arguments have been forced, so an error raised by the intrinsic takes the location of whatever annotated code ran last. Seen in SET.ADD, SET.REMOVE, VEC.OF and SET.OF: errors/152_set_element_type_mismatch moves from 1:11 to 1:29 when set.from-list stops being a prelude fold; '∅ set.add([1, 2, 3] vec.of)' already shows it on master. Fix: capture the call-site annotation before forcing arguments, or attach it from the intrinsic's own Smid. Engine area (src/eval/stg/, machine): eucalypt-backend and eucalypt-diagnostics skills.
design: Root cause: a case continuation (Branch / BranchPredecoded, and FusedPrimopLeft/Right) captures state.annotation when pushed but does not restore it when it resumes, unlike SeqBind. An intrinsic's inlined wrapper forces its arguments through case/force, so by the time Op::Bif runs, state.annotation is whatever annotated code the argument evaluation last entered (e.g. the vec.of call inside set.add's argument). Fix: in return_data/return_native/return_fun, when one of those continuations resumes successfully (branch body, fallback, or next fused operand / fused BIF), restore its push-time annotation with set_annotation, exactly as SeqBind does (including an invalid Smid, per eu-og3u6; last_annotation remains the fallback). Error paths (NoBranchForDataTag/Native) are left as they are. This is general, not per-intrinsic: it fixes SET.ADD, SET.REMOVE, VEC.OF, SET.OF and any other intrinsic (and eu-oaz72.64's family if the stale Smid was the cause). Gate: error fixtures for set.add/set.remove with a computed argument whose evaluation enters annotated code, checked in source and blob prelude modes; fault-injected by removing the restore. Every changed error snapshot explained in the PR.
acceptance_criteria: Errors raised by these intrinsics point at the intrinsic's call site in both prelude modes; error-harness fixtures gate it (fault-injection verified).
notes:
BLOCKED on a policy decision (2026-11-13). Root cause confirmed: Branch/BranchPredecoded/FusedPrimopLeft/Right capture state.annotation at push but never restore it on resume (SeqBind does), so a BIF's machine.annotation() is whatever annotated code its argument evaluation last entered. The general fix (restore the push-time annotation on every successful resume, ~40 lines in src/eval/bytecode/machine.rs return_data/return_native/return_fun) fixes set.add/vec.of (152 and 'set.add([1,2,3] vec.of)' both move to 1:11) but changes 19 source-prelude error snapshots and breaks gates: (a) diagnostics corpus provocations/metadata_span primary moves from 3:1 to 2:27 (2:23 with the Branch-only restore), violating its pinned region 3..3 from eu-1tkk.7.34 -- master's line 3 comes from the stale annotation itself; (b) harness test errors/229_1tkk_7_38_underapplied_call_span fails; (c) 011_assert_pred primary moves from the failing '>' (1:14) to '//=?' (1:8); 078 loses its trace frame; others: 080, 082, 108, 149, 192, 241 x2, 250 x4, 263, 271, catenation_arith. So the stale annotation is acting as a crude 'where the bad value came from' pointer that several pinned locations rely on. Decision needed: (1) adopt the lexical-annotation policy and re-baseline those snapshots, including loosening metadata_span (owner only, since the ratchet only tightens); or (2) a targeted fix that keeps the stale annotation everywhere except the set/vec element-check errors (it would need a marker on intrinsic wrapper forcing, a special case the Architecture criterion would flag); or (3) close as by-design. Not pushed; no PR.
2026-11-13 implementation: owner decision 21 adopts the general fix. Restore push-time annotation (set_annotation, as SeqBind) on every successful resume of Branch / BranchPredecoded / FusedPrimopLeft / FusedPrimopRight in return_data/return_native/return_fun; error paths unchanged. Re-baseline changed error snapshots (incl. diagnostics metadata_span pinned region, errors/229) with a report table under docs/superpowers/reports/. Possible follow-ups: carry operand Smid with errors to recover under-applied-call span; NoBranchForNative still uses state.annotation; DeMeta/LookupLitForce resume without restore; vec.of element error says 'expected set'.

title: (BUG) String interpolation parsing: padded format spec looks up 'up ', '{ a b }' silently evaluates as {a}
description: Non-blocking review findings on eu-oaz72.3 (PR #1148), both predating it. (1) A padded function-style format spec breaks: "{ s : up }" looks up "up " with the trailing space because format_content keeps it; trim spec whitespace. (2) "{ a b }" silently evaluates as {a} with no diagnostic; it should be an error. (3) Hardening: debug_assert that tree length equals source length where LSP code slices the source with tree ranges (src/driver/lsp/actions.rs, formatting.rs, diagnostics.rs). Regression tests fault-injection verified.
design:
Design (implementation lane):
(1) Lexer: StringPatternLexer/CStringPatternLexer format_content stops before trailing whitespace (internal whitespace such as printf '% d' kept); the trailing run is emitted as WHITESPACE trivia, so the tree stays lossless and the spec token is exact. Parser adds trivia after the spec. "{ s : up }" then looks up 'up'.

Covers "{a b}", "{x:.2f}" (spec silently dropped today), "{x:a:b}". None of these is documented as valid: docs/guide/string-interpolation.md says braces take names and dotted lookups. Wired into syntax/error.rs, LSP diagnostics, wasm_pipeline.
(3) LSP: debug_assert tree length == source length in code_actions and format_range; debug_assert range end within source in text_range_to_lsp_range.
Tests: error fixture in tests/harness/errors, harness checks in an existing string-interpolation topic file, lexer/parser unit tests, highlighting corpus check.

title: Design effect-constrained mutable storage, transients, or a memo combinator
description:
Owner decision 2026-11-11: put on the roadmap. Purpose: O(1) in-place update for workloads with 1e7+ indexed updates (AoC 2020 d23 cups, 2018 d9 marbles, 2020 d15, 2017 d5, 2018 d14; Intcode at scale), which no persistent structure reaches. Two candidate models to evaluate:
(a) Effect-confined mutable storage, like Haskell ST/STArray: mutable arrays (and possibly dicts) created and used only inside a { :do } / { :state } block where sequencing is explicit, frozen to an immutable value on exit; no mutable value escapes.
(b) Clojure-style transients: a persistent dict/vec converted to a transient, updated in place by a single owner, then made persistent again; needs a guarantee (runtime ownership check or type-level) that the transient is not shared or reused after update - harder under laziness, where evaluation order is not the textual order.
Design must address: laziness and thunk capture of a mutable value, GC (storage in the GC heap per the eu-oaz72.5 rule, write barriers if the generational GC needs them), the bytecode engine, type checker support, element types (primitives first or any value), and the interaction with par-* process parallelism. Gate: worth building only once per-step loop cost has been brought well below a microsecond (eu-oaz72.4 GC policy, eu-oaz72.27 strict accumulation) - measure first. Related: eu-oaz72.23 (persistent vector), eu-oaz72.21 (dict).
acceptance_criteria: Design note in docs/superpowers/plans comparing (a) effect-confined mutable storage, (b) transients and (c) memo combinator, with semantics, examples (a cups-style 1e7-update program; a stones-style discovered-state memo), GC and laziness analysis, and go/no-go gates tied to measured loop throughput; ROADMAP entry added.
notes:
2026-11-11 owner decision: third candidate folded in.
(c) memo(f) combinator: f: memo(g) caches g's results inside the function value; the mutation is invisible because f(k) always equals g(k). Target: memoisation where states are discovered during recursion (AoC 2024 d11 stones, non-enumerable search states), which a lazy self-referential dict (eu-oaz72.21, decision 3) cannot do because its key set is fixed at construction. Design points: cache storage in the GC heap (eu-oaz72.5 rule), keys as dict keys (primitives and lists of primitives), interaction with par-* (each forked worker has its own cache), re-entrancy when g recursively calls f on a thunk that is mid-evaluation, cache growth and lifetime (tied to the function value's reachability), and the bytecode engine. Pure alternatives to compare: threading a dict through recursion or { :state } (works today once dict exists; clumsy and needs strict accumulation, eu-oaz72.27), and a lazy infinite trie over the key space (MemoTrie-style; fine for ints, awkward for lists/strings, memory-heavy).
Enumerable-state memoisation needs nothing new beyond eu-oaz72.21 plus a cookbook example (eu-oaz72.16).

title: Exact diagnostic for pipeline (catenation) precedence and lone-anaphor scope mistakes
description:
Catenation (pipeline juxtaposition) has precedence 20. Every operator above it (↑ . calls ! ¬ ✓ ∘ ; ^ !! * / ÷ % + - < > <= >= ++ << <$> = != && ∧ || ∨, user operators at default 50) becomes a whole operand of the pipeline step on either side: `c nth(0) = 1` cooks to `=(nth(0), 1)(c)`; `k + 1 inc` to `inc(+(k, 1))`. Operators below it (=> ⇒ 15, @ 10, // //<< //= //=> //=? //=?> //! 5) wrap the finished pipeline: `c nth(0) //=> 1` cooks to `//=>(nth(0)(c), 1)` - correct and outside this bug. Verified with eu dump cooked.

The mistake produces two runtime failure shapes, both must be covered:
(a1) the operator's result is called: `c nth(i) = 2` -> 'tried to call a false as a function'.
(a2) the operator receives the step's partially applied function as an operand: `v vec.nth(0) + 1` -> 'type mismatch: expected number, found a function' raised inside +.
Exact trigger: the failing application / operand comes from a catenation whose operand is an infix-operator expression written without parentheses in the source. Then state the parse as fact, e.g. "`c nth(i) = 2` was read as `c (nth(i) = 2)`; parenthesise the pipeline: `(c nth(i)) = 2`". No compile-time warning: an operator operand may legitimately yield a function (`c nth(0) ∘ k`). The left-hand form (`x + y f` = f(x + y)) can silently give a different value with no error; out of scope (docs).
Needs: a catenation-origin marker and the operator expression span carried from cook to runtime, and parenthesisation from the rowan tree.

(b) Lone anaphor: an expression anaphor whose lambda body is only the anaphor (`nth(_)` = nth(λx. x)) is the identity function, known at desugar. Report as fact, as a note on a following runtime error at least (owner to choose whether also a check-time warning): "`_` in `nth(_)` makes nth's argument the identity function; its scope ends at these parentheses".

Related: eu-oaz72.28 (remove/gate the existing broad hints).
acceptance_criteria: Diagnostics corpus tests spanning the scope: (a1) and (a2) with each operator band above 20 (=, +, &&, ++, <$>, ∘ where it fails, user operator), on both sides of catenation, nested pipelines, inside blocks, args and anaphoric lambdas; negative cases that must NOT get the note: parenthesised `c (nth(i) = 2)`, //= //=> // => @ after pipelines, legitimate `c f ∘ g`, ordinary not-callable and type-mismatch errors with no catenation, operator on the left of catenation; (b) positive and negative (`_ + 1`, `f(_, 1)` sections) cases. Fault-injection verified.

title: Diagnostic hints chosen by value type or name shape alone fire on unrelated mistakes
description:
Several hints are attached purely on the runtime type of the failing value or the shape of a name, with no evidence from the source, so they appear on mistakes they have nothing to do with and send the reader the wrong way.

Instances:
- src/eval/error.rs not_callable_notes, true/false: always adds "note: 'and' and 'or' are identifiers in eucalypt, not logical operators ...". Seen on `(cells vec.nth(i) = "S")` and `filter(cells vec.nth(_) = "S")`, neither of which contains and/or.
- same function, number/string/symbol/datetime/empty list: always adds a catenation note whose example is wrong ("'f(a) + 1' binds as 'f(a + 1)'": f(a) + 1 on its own is (f(a)) + 1; the trap is `x f(a) + 1`, read as `x (f(a) + 1)`).
- src/eval/stg/compiler.rs unresolved variable: any single-letter name gets "eucalypt has no arrow functions; '->' is the const operator" (seen for an unresolved import name `g` with no '->' anywhere).
- not_callable_notes true/false: 'if this result of a boolean expression, check operator precedence' (also ungrammatical).

Rule to adopt: a hint is shown only when the source gives evidence for it (the identifier and/or appears in the failing expression; '->' appears in the declaration; etc.), or it states a fact about the actual program (what was parsed, what was called) rather than a guess. Audit every hint/help/note site in src/eval/error.rs, src/eval/stg/compiler.rs and the diagnostic renderers against this rule.
acceptance_criteria: Every hint site audited and either gated on source evidence, rewritten as a factual statement, or removed (list in the PR); the four instances above no longer appear without their trigger; diagnostics corpus tests for the gated and ungated cases, fault-injection verified.
close_reason: Merged in PR #1160 (merge commit a673893). Hints are shown only on source evidence. Evidence is read as tokens from the eucalypt lexer, so strings and comments never count. The catenation-precedence note was removed rather than kept on a copied precedence table; restoring it would need the cooked fixities carried into diagnostics.

title: String intrinsics: str.md5, str.code-points / str.from-code-points, ch.code-point / ch.of-code-point
description: Only str.sha256 exists. MD5 is required by 2015 d4, 2016 d5/d14/d17. No char-code conversion (ord/chr). No radix parse ('0xff' num errors; no %b format) for hex/binary inputs (2021 d16 etc.).
acceptance_criteria: str.md5 matches RFC 1321 test vectors; str.code-points / str.from-code-points round-trip ASCII and non-ASCII text; ch.code-point / ch.of-code-point consistent with them; errors for invalid code points (surrogates, > 0x10FFFF); docs, types, grammar prelude name lists updated.
notes:
2026-11-11: radix parsing and bit-string helpers move to the AoC helper library (outside this repo); %b moves to the str.format bead. Remaining: str.md5, ord/chr.
2026-11-12 owner naming decision: str.code-points(s) -> list of ints (Unicode scalar values, one per character as split by str.letters) and str.from-code-points(ns) -> string; single-character ch.code-point(c) and ch.of-code-point(n) in the existing ch namespace. ('codes' rejected as ambiguous between bytes, UTF-16 units and code points.) str.md5(s) returns lowercase hex like str.sha256. No puzzle-shaped hashing intrinsics (stretched MD5, nonce search): high-volume MD5 days (2016 d5, d14) are bound by loop cost, eu-oaz72.4 / eu-oaz72.27. A UTF-8 str.bytes is a possible later addition, not in scope.
2026-11-15 design (lane agent): five intrinsics MD5, CODE_POINTS, FROM_CODE_POINTS, CODE_POINT, OF_CODE_POINT -> str.md5, str.code-points, str.from-code-points, ch.code-point, ch.of-code-point (names/types fixed by the 2026-11-12 decision). md5 via the md-5 crate (RustCrypto, same Digest API as sha2); hex lowercase, over UTF-8 bytes like sha256. Code points = char as u32 per str.letters. Choices left open by the bead, to be listed in the PR: (1) one new ExecutionError::InvalidCodePoint 'invalid code point: ...' for: from-code-points / of-code-point given a non-whole number, a negative, >0x10FFFF or a surrogate (0xD800-0xDFFF); (2) ch.code-point on a string that is not exactly one character is the same error variant (length stated); (3) from-code-points on a non-number element is the ordinary type mismatch.

title: Strict accumulation: foldl-strict and demand analysis for self-recursive accumulators
description: A counter loop to 1e6 grows the stack two frames per iteration because the accumulator stays lazy; forcing it in the condition gives O(1) stack. 1e6-step simulations take 3-20 s and 2-11 GB; 1e7 is out of reach. A `seq`/strict-fold primitive (or demand analysis proving strictness for self-recursive accumulators) would make tight loops viable.
design:
Design (2026-11-12, implementing agent):
1. Demand analysis (src/core/analyse_demand.rs):
 a. Signature frames: a stack parallel to de Bruijn scopes (one frame per Let/Lam). A saturated call through Var::Bound to a let-bound lambda uses that binding's signature (pessimistic lazy_multi when unknown or partially applied).
 b. analyse_let analyses RHSs before the body. Lambda bindings start from an optimistic signature (strict_once per parameter) and the RHSs are re-analysed until every lambda binding's signature is stable (joint fixpoint over the let group; only iterates when a RHS consulted the group's own signatures). Stale pointer-keyed signatures from discarded iterations are rolled back. Iteration cap: on reaching it, signatures are set pessimistic and the group analysed once more (a post-fixpoint, so sound).
 c. IF: a variable strict in both branches is strict (branch lub on strictness only; cardinality unchanged, conservative).
 d. Lambda value (not directly applied): captured variables are Lazy, not the body's strictness unscaled. Fixes the #1156 open note, observable on master: k(a): {y: •}.(a + y); k(panic("x")) block? panics.
 Loop A, loop(a, n): if(n = 0, a, loop(a + 1, n - 1)), then has a strict -> the recursive call Seqs a + 1.
2. Prelude: foldl-strict(op, i, l), same signature as foldl, forcing the accumulator to WHNF each step (owner decision on this bead + plan s6). foldl unchanged. sum, product, count use foldl-strict (observably identical: + and * are strict, count never forces elements).
Untouched: lambda literal in function position signature lookup keyed on the pre-analysis body pointer (#1156 note 2).
acceptance_criteria: foldl-strict documented and typed, range(0, 1e6) foldl-strict(+, 0) in constant stack and fewer ticks than foldl; foldl behaviour unchanged (test with a lazy accumulator that relies on it); demand analysis makes loop A's accumulator strict (stack and ticks measured before/after under the protocol); tests fault-injection verified.
notes: 2026-11-12 owner decisions: foldl must NOT change (keep its lazy accumulator semantics). Provide a separate strict variant named foldl-strict (foldl' is not possible: a single quote starts a quoted identifier). Second part: demand analysis should prove self-recursive accumulators strict (loop A in the if/then bug: 2 extra frames/iter from the a + 1 + 1 ... chain) - a compiler improvement, not a language feature. A seq primitive only if that proves insufficient. Related: the if/then tail-position bug (constant stack is a prerequisite for measuring this).

description: + and * error past i64; ^ goes to float. Puzzles such as 2023 d24 part 2, CRT combinations and some product-of-cycle answers exceed i64. Decide between promotion to bignum and an explicit bigint type.

notes: 2026-11-12 owner decision: restructured. December scope: intrinsics mulmod(a, b, m), powmod(b, e, m), modinv(a, m) computing in i128 internally so a*b%m and modular exponentiation are exact for i64 operands and moduli (AoC 2019 d22 p2 modulus ~1.2e14, 2020 d13 CRT, generic modpow). Values stay i64; no change to the number representation. modpow and CRT move here from the general prelude helper list (eu-oaz72.26) because they need i128 to be correct; CRT can be prelude on top of mulmod/modinv. comments.text: Design (PR a, eu-oaz72.24/modular-intrinsics): three new intrinsics MULMOD, POWMOD, MODINV in src/eval/stg/arith.rs, appended to the catalogue (num → num → num [→ num], all args strict), exposed as top-level prelude functions mulmod(a, b, m), powmod(b, e, m), modinv(a, m) beside mod/quot/rem, typed number → … → number. All operands must be integers in the i64 range; arithmetic is in i128 (a and b reduced mod m before multiplying, so |product| < 2^126), so results are exact for any i64 operands and moduli. Results are normalised into [0, m) — negative operands give the non-negative residue. Errors, through one new ExecutionError::ModularArithmetic(Smid, String) ('modular arithmetic: …' with a help line): a modulus m <= 0; a non-integer operand; a negative exponent to powmod; modinv(a, m) when gcd(a, m) != 1 (message names a, m and the gcd). m = 1 gives 0 everywhere (modinv(a, 1) = 0). powmod(b, 0, m) = 1 mod m. powmod is square-and-multiply over mulmod; modinv is extended Euclid in i128. Choices the owner decision leaves implicit and this PR takes (flagged in the PR body): errors for m <= 0 and for a negative exponent (rather than inverting), non-integer operands rejected rather than truncated. title: Emacs mode: run, test, check and target commands that work from the file's location
description: Today only eucalypt-render-buffer / -region exist, piping text to `eu eu@-`: imports resolve from default-directory/project root rather than the file, there is no eu test, target selection (-t, via eu list-targets), eu check, -e, or eu fmt, ANSI colour codes fill *Eucalypt Errors* (set NO_COLOR), and output-format detection string-matches "-j" against the whole command (paths containing -j match).
design:
Design (eu-oaz72.19):
- Shared runner: every command runs eu on the visited file's path (file-local-name, so TRAMP works), with default-directory set to the file's directory, and process-environment extended with NO_COLOR=1 and TERM=dumb so no ANSI escapes reach Emacs. Unsaved buffers are offered for save first (compile's save-some-buffers behaviour).
- eucalypt-run (C-c C-c): eu FILE, stdout to *Eucalypt Output* (yaml/json/text mode inferred from tokenised args), stderr to *Eucalypt Errors* in eucalypt-compilation-mode. C-u edits the command.
- eucalypt-run-target (C-c C-r): completing-read over 'eu list-targets FILE', then eu FILE -t TARGET.
- eucalypt-evaluate (C-c C-e): eu FILE -e EXPR, read from the minibuffer with history.
- eucalypt-test (C-c C-t) / eucalypt-check (C-c C-v): eu test FILE / eu check FILE via compile in eucalypt-compilation-mode (recompile with g).
- eucalypt-compilation-mode: compilation-mode derivative whose error regexp matches codespan's '┌─ PATH:LINE:COL' locations, so errors are clickable; paths resolve from the file's directory.
- Render buffer/region keep piping stdin but use the same environment, file-directory cwd and error mode; output-format inference tokenises the command (split-string-shell-command) and looks for -j/--json and -x/--export FMT tokens, so paths containing -j no longer match.
- Tests: ERT file editors/emacs/test/eucalypt-mode-commands-test.el, batch, no network, driven by a stub eu script that records argv, cwd and env; plus an optional real-eu check when an eu binary is given. Run from scripts/check-emacs-mode.sh (which CI does not run; no CI wiring needed).
acceptance_criteria: Commands for eu FILE -t TARGET (completing targets), eu test FILE, eu check FILE, run on the visited file's path; errors buffer free of escape codes and clickable via compilation-mode; batch tests.

title: Docs: Advent of Code cookbook
description:
No AoC-oriented guide exists. Write docs/guide/advent-of-code.md (and add to SUMMARY.md), drawn from docs/eucalypt-style.md and examples/aoc25:
1. Running: per-day targets with `import: "input=inputs/dayNN.txt"`, a `:test` target on the example input (without one `eu test` judges the default output and reports FAIL), `-e` exploration, eu check.
2. Parsing: lines, blank-line blocks (split-on(= "")), ints incl. negatives (str.matches-of + num), regex groups (str.match-with), chars (str.letters), destructuring params.
3. Grids: vec.of + y*W+x, arr.*, neighbours via { :for }, transpose, find a char, bounds.
4. Search: BFS template (frontier + set of encoded coords), Dijkstra template (state the current lack of a priority queue), graph.union-find / topo-sort.
5. Memoisation & DP: lazy self-referential structures, fold DP tables, cost of block merge/lookup.
6. Iteration: tail recursion vs iterate (head retention), cycle detection.
7. Intervals and geometry.
8. Debugging: ▶, dbg, ` :trace, eu dump, -S, --heap-limit-mib, timeout.
9. Performance: what is O(1)/O(n) (vec, set, block lookup), par-*.
All examples tested by scripts/test-doc-examples.py.
acceptance_criteria: Page published in the book with tested examples covering each section; linked from the cheat sheet.

title: num rejects numbers with leading zeros ("07", "-07") and the error caret points at the wrong call
description: `eu -e '{a: "07" num}'` -> bad number format: 07. Same for "00", "-07". Fixed-width numeric fields with leading zeros are common in puzzle inputs. In a pipeline (`str.letters map(num)`) the caret pointed at `str` rather than `num`. Accepting leading zeros may count as a semantic change - confirm with the owner before merging.
design: Leading zeros: NUMPARSE (src/eval/stg/string.rs) keeps serde_json::Number as the one number grammar. A new helper strips redundant leading zeros from the integer part only (after an optional '-'), keeping one digit, before parsing: "07"->7, "-07"->-7, "00"->0, "007.5"->7.5. Always decimal, never octal. Anything else serde rejects is still rejected ("+7", " 7", "0x1f", "", "-"). Tests: extend tests/harness/032_number_parse.eu with gated checks; fault-inject by removing the strip. Docs: num's doc string is in lib/prelude.eu (held by another lane) so it is left; docs/reference/prelude/numbers.md is generated. Caret: the in-function case (f(s): s num, called inline) is fixed by eu-oaz72.63's resume-annotation change (now points at the call). The point-free pipeline case (str.letters map(num)) has no location at all: the global NUMPARSE wrapper carries only the intrinsic's synthetic Smid and no user frame is on the stack or env chain. Fixing that needs the compiler to annotate unapplied intrinsic references at the use site (compiler lane) - reported as follow-up, not done here. Semantic: accepting leading zeros is a change to what num accepts; no owner decision recorded, so the PR is held for the owner.
acceptance_criteria: "07" num = 7 (or an explicit decision recorded otherwise); caret on the failing num call; tests.
notes: 2026-11-14 owner decision (to coordinator 5): leading zeros read as decimal accepted, on condition that num rejects hex-prefixed strings (0x...), since accepting 0x would suggest 0... is octal. Lane extends #1193; hold stays until the owner releases it.

title: LSP lifecycle defects: no exit after shutdown, deferred diagnostics, invalid params kill the server
design:
1. Exit: main_loop takes the Connection by value and drops it before io_threads.join(), so the stdout writer thread ends. Shutdown handled in our loop (not Connection::handle_shutdown, which errors on any non-exit message): reply null, then answer further requests with InvalidRequest until `exit`. exit after shutdown or stdin EOF -> code 0; exit without shutdown -> code 1 (LSP spec).
2. Diagnostics: pipeline results travel on a crossbeam channel; main loop uses select! over the client receiver and the pipeline receiver, so results are applied (and diagnostics published) without waiting for client traffic. crossbeam-channel becomes a direct dependency (already in Cargo.lock via lsp-server).
3. Invalid params: a generic request helper turns ExtractError::JsonError into an InvalidParams (-32602) response; notifications with bad params are logged and ignored instead of propagating with `?`.
4. Refresh: record workspace.inlayHint.refreshSupport and workspace.semanticTokens.refreshSupport from InitializeParams; send each refresh only when advertised, with unique request ids.
Tests: new tests/lsp_stdio_test.rs driving `eu lsp` over stdio (existing lsp tests are in-process and cannot see transport/lifecycle). No .eu program can reach the LSP loop, so no harness test.
acceptance_criteria: Server exits 0 promptly after shutdown/exit; diagnostics are published without further client traffic; invalid params return InvalidParams; refresh requests gated on client capabilities; LSP tests for each.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #1186 (merged): exit after shutdown/exit or stdin close, idle diagnostics via select over pipeline results, InvalidParams for bad params, refresh gated on client refreshSupport. Stdio tests in tests/lsp_stdio_test.rs, fault-injection verified.

title: ProtoLet drops the Core Let's own smid, so a Let-bodied thunk has no Ann to find
description:
Found by clarion while fixing eu-7fjiq (PR #1100). A COMPILER-side gap, distinct from eu-7fjiq's runtime one, and it is why eu-7fjiq's own verification criterion could not be met.

eu-7fjiq fixed target_annotation to look THROUGH a leading Let/LetRec to find an Ann. That fix is real and verified on all three engine paths. But for tests/harness/errors/error_176.eu the binding 'result' has a thunk body of the shape Let(__shared_e = ..., EXPECT(...)) with NO Ann anywhere inside it, so there is nothing for the widened lookup to find. ProtoLet in src/eval/stg/compiler.rs never reads the Core Let's own smid, so the annotation is lost at COMPILE time rather than at lookup time.

PROTOTYPE ATTEMPTED AND REVERTED, which is the useful part of this report. Wrapping ProtoLet's output in Ann whenever the Let's own smid is valid broke primary-location attribution broadly: unrelated outer Lets also carry valid smids - block desugaring emits a whole-file Let, for instance - so the naive fix mis-attributes the primary label across the corpus. Any real fix needs to distinguish a Let that stands for a user-meaningful construct from one that is a desugaring artefact. Do not simply re-try the naive version.

SECOND, INDEPENDENT REASON error_176 loses its frame: its error propagates through evaluate_to_whnf (EXPECT's render_debug_repr_forced), which restores the caller's stack BEFORE propagating the error - see the pre-existing test test_evaluate_to_whnf_impl_restores_caller_state_before_propagating_error. So even with a correct Ann, that particular fixture would still lose the frame at error time. Fixing the ProtoLet gap alone will NOT restore error_176's secondary label; both paths need addressing, or a different fixture is needed to demonstrate the improvement.

IMPACT: silent loss of the secondary 'called from here' label and stack trace on diagnostics whose thunk body is a binding group. Source-prelude only in the one observed case; blob mode was byte-identical across the corpus. Not release-gating for 0.14 - the owner ruled the related engine divergence non-blocking on 2026-07-31 and this is narrower still.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A Core Let that stands for a user-meaningful construct carries its smid through ProtoLet so the enclosing thunk has an Ann to find, WITHOUT mis-attributing primary labels for desugaring-artefact Lets (block desugaring's whole-file Let is the known counter-example). 2. The full errors/ corpus captured before and after in BOTH prelude modes, with every moved diagnostic individually explained. 3. A harness regression test that genuinely gates, fault-injection verified per CLAUDE.md, anchored on the primary-label line. 4. Either error_176.eu regains its secondary label and trace - which also requires addressing the evaluate_to_whnf stack restoration - or the PR states plainly which fixture demonstrates the fix and why error_176 cannot.

title: beta_reduce: make the occurrence count lambda-depth aware (occ_in_lam)
description:
Follow-up FIX bead for the defect eu-6xgtk established and measured. eu-6xgtk was scoped to a reachability verdict only and is closed; this bead carries the fix.

DEFECT: #1086 (eu-gua64) let-binds an argument when 'uses > 1 && !duplicable(arg)'. free_var_occurrences (src/core/inline/reduce.rs:237) is a raw syntactic count via visit_free_vars with no lambda awareness, so a binder occurring once syntactically but UNDER an inner lambda counts as uses == 1, is substituted, and is then re-evaluated once per application of that lambda. GHC guards exactly this with an occ_in_lam flag on OneOcc; preInlineUnconditionally requires OneOcc AND not-in-lambda (Peyton Jones and Marlow, 'Secrets of the Glasgow Haskell Compiler inliner', JFP 2002, section 3).

MEASURED COST (stopwatch, clean rig, master 642b5e2d, blob mode, no metadata): treatment N-slope = 32.0 x K exactly at every grid point (K=1 -> 32.0, K=5 -> 160.0, K=20 -> 640.0, K=80 -> 2560.0) against a control at a flat 32.0. Substituting the raw expression costs exactly K times the shared-Var control.

FIX SHAPE: count occurrences with lambda depth, treating an occurrence under a Lam as more-than-once for work-safety purposes, so the existing 'uses > 1' guard let-binds it. Do not change duplicable() - a Var, Literal or Intrinsic under a lambda is still free to substitute.

SILENT PERF ONLY, no wrong answers, bounded by application count (not exponential, unlike eu-gua64). Pre-existing: this shape was substituted before #1086 and in 0.13.2.

*** RELEASE-WINDOW HAZARD - READ BEFORE SCHEDULING *** Changing beta_reduce changes inliner output, therefore blob content, therefore baked global Smids. That is the exact mechanism behind eu-7x0r, eu-r4647 and the closed #1090, and it would disturb the diagnostics chain merged for 0.14 and invalidate #1085's blessed golden snapshots, which are the release-gate evidence. Not to be landed inside the 0.14 merge window without an explicit owner decision. Recommended as an early-0.15 item, or early-0.14 only if the owner accepts a re-bless of the goldens.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Occurrence counting in src/core/inline/reduce.rs is lambda-depth aware, so a single occurrence under a Lam no longer passes the uses<=1 substitution path for a non-duplicable argument. 2. A harness regression test using the eu-6xgtk shape (self-recursive higher-order combinator, parameter referenced once inside an anaphoric lambda, not re-threaded through the recursive call), fault-injection verified per CLAUDE.md, and written with NO metadata on any binding so it is not confounded by eu-bc34x. 3. Measured: the treatment fixture's N-slope becomes independent of K, matching the control's flat slope. 4. Golden diagnostic snapshots re-blessed and the diff explained, or the change deferred per the release-window hazard above.

title: (BUG) c-string with doubled braces silently drops the whole declaration
description:
Found while writing fixtures for eu-1z503 (furnace, 2026-07-27).

A declaration whose value is a c-string containing doubled braces vanishes
from the output entirely — no error, no warning, exit 0:

    $ printf 'a: c"{{X}}"\n' > f.eu
    $ eu f.eu
    ---
    {}
    EXIT=0

Expected either the escaped form '{X}' (as the plain string "{{X}}" gives)
or a parse error. Producing an empty document and claiming success is the
worst of the three.

Plain strings handle it correctly:

    b: "{{X}}"            -> "{X}"      correct
    c: c"\u007bX\u007d"    -> "{X}"      correct (workaround)
    a: c"{{X}}"           -> declaration GONE

docs/guide/string-interpolation.md documents '{{' and '}}' as the literal
brace escape and says c-strings are the C-escape variant, so a reader has
every reason to expect the c-string form to work.

SEVERITY: silent data loss of a whole declaration, which is the class this
cycle keeps finding. A user interpolating literal braces into a c-string
gets a silently empty result rather than a diagnostic.

WANTED: make '{{'/'}}' work inside c-strings, or reject the form with a
parse error. Either is fine; disappearing is not. Plus a harness fixture.

WORKAROUND in use: \u007b / \u007d, as in tests/harness/193_non_text_block_keys.eu.
design:
OWNER DIRECTION (2026-07-27, stated as 'probably', so treat as a strong steer to be confirmed on implementation, not a settled spec):

'Backslash is the escaping protocol for braces in c-strings. So that is probably illegal and ought to be an error.'

THE COHERENT MODEL THIS IMPLIES: c-strings escape with backslash, so a literal brace is '\{' and '\}'. The '{{' / '}}' doubling is the RAW-string escape and has no meaning in a c-string. Therefore 'c"{{X}}"' is a malformed interpolation, not an escape, and must be DIAGNOSED rather than silently yielding an empty declaration.

WORK REQUIRED, in this order:
1. VERIFY THE PREMISE FIRST. Does '\{' currently work as a literal-brace escape in a c-string? If it does not, the escaping protocol is not yet what the model assumes and that gap is part of this bead. Check the lexer, do not infer from the docs.
2. Establish what a c-string currently does with single '{...}' - does it interpolate at all? The answer decides whether '{{' is 'malformed interpolation' or 'two literal braces'. Both routes end in a diagnostic here, but the message differs.
3. Make it an ERROR with a proper diagnostic and a source location on the offending construct - not a panic, not a silent drop. Silently producing an empty declaration is the one outcome that is wrong under every reading.
4. Document it in the C-Strings section of docs/guide/string-interpolation.md, which currently documents backslash escapes only and says nothing about braces. That silence is what made this ambiguous.
5. Harness fixture asserting the diagnostic and its location, plus a positive fixture for whatever the correct literal-brace spelling turns out to be. Assert VALUES and the error, not absence-of-error.

DO NOT start step 3 before steps 1 and 2 are answered and reported - the semantics decide the message, and this bead has already been mis-triaged twice by reasoning ahead of evidence.
notes:
STATUS CORRECTED TWICE BY THE COORDINATOR - read this before acting.

FIRST ERROR: filed/escalated P1 as 'silent data loss, a documented form eats a declaration', relaying an agent's framing without checking the docs.
SECOND ERROR: closed as 'NOT A BUG, expected documented behaviour', citing docs/guide/string-interpolation.md:156-163 on numbered string anaphora. That passage does not cover this case either.

THE ACTUAL POSITION, established with the owner: the '{{' / '}}' literal-brace escape is documented at docs/guide/string-interpolation.md:36 in the RAW STRINGS section. The C-Strings section begins at line 39 and documents C-style backslash escapes only; it says NOTHING about braces, interpolation or brace escaping. So the behaviour of '{{' inside a c-string is UNSPECIFIED - neither clearly correct nor clearly a defect.

OBSERVED: 'a: c"{{X}}"' renders as '{}' with exit 0. The plain-string form '"{{X}}"' correctly yields '{X}'. Note single braces are numbered string anaphora and make the literal define a FUNCTION, which is unserialisable and correctly omitted from output - so an empty render is the expected symptom of 'this became a function', and the question is whether doubled braces in a c-string should have escaped instead.

THE REAL QUESTION, which is a SPECIFICATION question not a bug report: do c-strings support brace interpolation at all? If they do, '{{' must escape as it does elsewhere and this is a defect. If they do not, then '{' and '{{' should be literal characters in a c-string, and the current behaviour is ALSO wrong because it is treating them as anaphora. Either way, silently producing an empty declaration is a poor outcome - the three defensible behaviours are interpolate, escape, or diagnose.

WHAT IS NEEDED FIRST: an owner decision on the intended semantics of braces in c-strings, then a doc change in the C-Strings section stating it explicitly, then a fixture pinning it. Do not write a fix before the semantics are decided.

PROCESS LESSON: a claim about .eu language behaviour is not established by reading a nearby passage. Quote the passage that governs the exact construct, or state that the docs are silent.
close_reason: Fixed: a: c"{{X}}" is now a parse error (exit 1), not a silently dropped declaration; the C-strings docs cover interpolation and \{ \} escapes

title: [bug] a user file named after a baked-in resource, absent from the lib path, is silently served the LIBRARY text instead of raising an import error
description:
Found by wicket reviewing PR #1080 (eu-8a49h), finding A residual hazard. PRE-EXISTING; not introduced or worsened by that PR.

read_fs_input's baked-in-resource fallback keys on the FILENAME STEM. So if a user writes 'import: "test.eu"' (or lens.eu, state.eu, reflect.eu, markup.eu, or 'package'/'build-meta' by stem) and that file is NOT found on the lib path or relative to cwd, they are silently served the SHIPPED LIBRARY TEXT instead of getting an import error.

Silent wrong behaviour: the user believes they imported their own module, and instead gets eucalypt's library. No diagnostic, no warning.

PR #1080 makes it marginally more discoverable - diagnostics now decline to blame a line inside the substituted text - but the substitution itself is untouched.

WANTED: a missing import should raise, not silently resolve to a same-stem baked-in resource. If the fallback must stay for compatibility, it should at minimum warn that a baked-in library was substituted for a file that was not found. Note the fallback IS load-bearing for legitimate uses - 'import: "prelude.eu"'-style filename imports of shipped libraries are supported and tested (test_lib_lens, test_lib_markup at tests/harness_test.rs:936,:951 run shipped libraries as the top-level subject) - so the fix must distinguish 'user meant the shipped library' from 'user meant their own missing file'.

title: [bug] 'eu check --strict' exits 0 on a hard CoreError originating in an IMPORTED file - the documented CI gate cannot catch it
description:
Found by wicket during review of PR #1077 (eu-mqlkv). PRE-EXISTING and general - not introduced by that PR.

SYMPTOM: the direct/imported asymmetry survives under eu check:
  eu check deep.eu     # fault present directly    -> exit 1
  eu check level2.eu   # SAME fault via an import  -> exit 0   (--strict makes no difference)

CAUSE: src/driver/check.rs:219 downgrades ANY pipeline failure to 'eu check: pipeline warning: ...' and contributes 0 to the error counts, so the exit code is determined by the phase-1 annotation scan of the BASE file alone. Anything that fails while translating an import is invisible to the exit code.

NOT limited to malformed annotations - wicket verified a circular import and a missing import file also exit 0 under eu check.

WHY IT MATTERS: CLAUDE.md documents 'eu check --strict' as THE CI gate ('use for CI gates'). It cannot currently be relied on to catch a hard CoreError originating in an imported library - arguably the more important half of eu-mqlkv, since libraries are exactly what you would gate in CI. This is the same failure class as eu-5yn9v: a gate that appears to work and does not. Documentation currently overstates what the gate provides.

Note exit 0 is still strictly better than the exit 101 panic the same input produced before PR #1077 - this is a gap, not a regression.

WANTED: pipeline failures during import translation should count toward eu check's error total (at minimum under --strict) so the exit code reflects them. Include regression tests for all three shapes wicket identified: malformed annotation via import, circular import, missing import file.

title: as-spec has no literal-type arm: s"\"prod\"" as-spec matches anything
description:
Found while implementing SV3 (eu-u9xj.1); the SV3 design spec flags it as
section 13.7 and calls it a probable defect in the shipped as-spec.

as-spec's to-spec-td (lib/prelude.eu, around 2245-2256) has NO arm for
:t-lit-str or :t-lit-sym, so both fall through to the any? default. Result:

  s"\"prod\"" as-spec   matches ANY value, not just the string "prod"
  s":ok" as-spec        matches ANY value, not just the symbol :ok

Literal types are a shipped surface (docs/guide/type-checking.md documents
them as subtypes of string/symbol, and the discriminated-union idiom in the
guide relies on them), so as-spec silently accepting anything where a literal
was specified defeats the purpose at exactly the point a user reaches for it.

SV3's validate DOES check literals by equality (design section 6.4), so the
two now genuinely disagree. This is deliberate per section 13.7 - SV3 does the
right thing on its own side rather than replicating the weaker behaviour - but
it means the SV3 as-spec-agreement harness corpus
(tests/harness/193_sv3_validate.eu) has to EXCLUDE literal types, and the
exclusion should not be permanent.

FIX: add :t-lit-str and :t-lit-sym arms to as-spec's to-spec-td, checking
equality against the literal, matching validate's lit-check. Design section
13.6 records the standing rule that as-spec and validate must never disagree
about what conforms, so extending one means extending the other - here
validate is already correct and only as-spec needs the arm.

Then extend 193_sv3_validate.eu's agreement corpus with literal-type pairs,
which will gate the two staying in step.

Regression test + fault injection required per CLAUDE.md.
notes: Blocked-adjacent context: SV3 (eu-u9xj.1, PR #1078) already implements the correct behaviour in validate, and its as-spec-agreement corpus in tests/harness/193_sv3_validate.eu excludes literal types solely because of this defect. Fixing this bead should remove that exclusion and add literal-type pairs to the corpus, which then gates the two implementations staying in step.

WICKET RULING on whether this should block PR #1078: NO - ship the divergence. Reasons: it is sanctioned by the approved spec (13.7); the underlying defect is filed and open (this bead); the test-corpus exclusion is DISCLOSED in the test file and PR body rather than hidden; and validate is the one behaving CORRECTLY (as-spec is the defective side). Fixing as-spec inside the same PR that changes the blob wire format would be worse review hygiene than shipping a documented, tracked divergence.

Wicket did ask for one thing: docs/guide/contracts.md currently states under 'What is not covered' that contracts and as-spec 'never disagree about what conforms'. That is now FALSE for literal types. A guide bullet pointing at this bead is being added so users meet the divergence in the guide rather than in a bead (finding F5).

See also eu-2yc1r: unifying the two interpreters behind validate would subsume this bead entirely.

title: IntrinsicMachine::force cannot memoise: an intrinsic forcing a lazy spine loses thunk updates
description:
Found while fixing the PP boundary check (furnace, 2026-07-26, PR #1075).

The machine memoises a thunk by writing the WHNF result back into the ENVIRONMENT SLOT that names it: vm.rs's Atom/Ref::L(i) path blackholes env slot i and pushes an Update continuation. 'IntrinsicMachine::force' takes an already-RESOLVED closure (AbiClosure) and calls evaluate_to_whnf on it — there is no slot, so nothing is written back and the thunk stays unevaluated in the heap.

Consequence: any intrinsic that forces a lazy list spine itself leaves every cell unmemoised. For a pure list that is only wasted work; for a single-pass source it is WRONG. Reproduced with par-map over a streaming import before the fix:
  { import: ["jl=jsonl-stream@testdata/aux_import.jsonl"] }
  a: jl par-map(_.name)   -> [Alice, Bob, Charlie]
  c: jl count             -> 1     (should be 3)
The par-map advanced the producer to exhaustion without memoising the cells, so the next reader re-forced the tail, got the exhausted producer's nil, and saw a one-element list.

Worked around in PR #1075 by forcing the spine in the PRELUDE first ('force-spine(xs): if((xs count) >= 0, xs, xs)'), which walks it through ordinary evaluation with proper updates, before __PARMAP sees it. That fixes par-* but not the general hazard: the next intrinsic that forces a spine will hit it again, and nothing gates against it.

Proper fix: give the neutral ABI an updating force — e.g. 'force_field(owner, idx)' that resolves the field, evaluates to WHNF and writes the result back into the owning env slot when the field ref is Ref::L(i). NOTE this is GC-subtle: the owner closure and its env are held across evaluate_to_whnf, which can collect and evacuate, so the owner must be rooted for the sub-run (the machine only stashes state.closure today). Design before implementing.

title: Source-prelude and blob-prelude differ in asymptotic complexity for the same definition
description:
Found while fixing eu-pazes (furnace, 2026-07-26). The pre-compiled prelude blob and the source-prelude fallback do not merely differ in constant factors — they differ in COMPLEXITY CLASS for the same prelude source.

Evidence, master release binary, same binary both ways:
  ./target/release/eu -e 'range(0,20000) max-of'                  -> 0.14s   (blob)
  ./target/release/eu --source-prelude -e 'range(0,22) max-of'    -> 7.01s   (source)
  ./target/release/eu --source-prelude -e 'range(0,24) max-of'    -> >60s    (source, timeout)
The blob path is linear; the source path is 2^N. The definition at the time was 'max-of(l): cond([... , max(l head, max-of(l tail))])' with 'max(l,r): if(l>r,l,r)' — r used twice. Under the blob some pass (inlining/sharing) makes the recursive thunk shared; under source compilation it is re-evaluated. A user-level COPY of the same definition is exponential in BOTH modes, so the blob is masking the bug in prelude code only.

Two consequences worth fixing independently of eu-pazes:
1. Anyone editing lib/prelude.eu invalidates the blob and silently switches every measurement to the slow path — this is exactly why the PR #1075 review measured 2^N while a master-based measurement saw linear. Measurements taken on a prelude-touching branch are not comparable with master's.
2. Any prelude definition with the same shape has a latent cliff that only appears in source-prelude mode (CI's 'Source-prelude harness' job).

Investigate which pass differs (candidates: the inliner, cluster inlining, or LetRec splitting seeded by the blob's unit interface) and either make the source path share equivalently, or add a tripwire that fails when a prelude definition's tick count diverges by more than a constant factor between the two modes. Note 'Source-prelude tick-parity tripwire' already exists (tests/tick_parity_test.rs) but did not catch this.
close_reason: Fixed: max-of is foldl-strict (0.30 s in both prelude modes at 20k); a user copy of the old shape is linear in both modes

comments.author: greg
comments.text:
MECHANISM IDENTIFIED (furnace, 2026-07-27, clean release build of master
a1af1f0b, same worktree measured in both configurations).

The divergence is inlining reach, and the difference is not a constant factor:

  range(1,20000) max-of   (master's then-current max-of)
    blob build:            153 ms          -> LINEAR
    source-prelude build:  no result in 90 s (2^N: 124/240/699/2568 ms for
                           N=16/18/20/22)  -> EXPONENTIAL

Same prelude source, same binary source, same machine.

`eu dump inlined` on a file whose only content is `main: range(1, 22) max-of`:

  source path — the prelude body is present and `max` has been beta-reduced
  into it, duplicating the recursive call:
    max-of = λ(l). COND([..., IF(GT(HEAD(l), max-of(TAIL(l))), HEAD(l),
                                 max-of(TAIL(l)))])

  blob path — the prelude combinator is an opaque baked global, never inlined:
    in let main = max-of(range(1, 22)) in { main: main }

So a prelude definition whose shape trips the inliner's work-duplication bug
(eu-gua64) is exponential on the source path and linear in blob mode. The
source-prelude CI jobs therefore exercise a materially different program, and a
complexity regression can be invisible in every blob job — which is exactly why
tests/harness/195_pazes_max_of_linear.eu is now run with `--source-prelude`.

Note also that `--source-prelude` at RUNTIME is not equivalent to a build with
no blob only in respect of where the prelude source comes from: the source text
is embedded at build time, so editing lib/prelude.eu and re-running with
`--source-prelude` has no effect without a rebuild. That cost a fault-injection
cycle here and is worth knowing before anyone else tries the same shortcut.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: Fixed: max-of is foldl-strict (0.30 s in both prelude modes at 20k); a user copy of the old shape is linear in both modes (owner grooming, 17 Nov; staleness check on master d1b867d). Owner: "go".

title: Lazy foldl retains the list it walks: flat (capture-trimmed) thunks plus selector thunks
description:
Split from eu-oaz72.175. With closed-binding (eu-oaz72.175's fix) count, foldl-strict and wrapper shapes run in constant space, but lazy foldl still retains the list: its accumulator thunk op(i, l head) is not forced until the end, and each thunk's env is the whole iteration frame (op, i, l), so the 200k-thunk chain holds every cell, including the dead slot l. Measured-single, 200k cells, closed-binding applied: foldl-strict 1,026 peak blocks, count 1,026, foldl 11,001, list-free lazy chain 3,513. Diagnosis: docs/superpowers/reports/2026-11-17-foldl-retention.md on branch eu-oaz72.175/foldl-trace.

A fix needs both flat (capture-trimmed) thunks, which owner decision 33 declined for now, and a selector-thunk rule (head/tail of an already-evaluated local cons becomes an alias of the field). Flat thunks change the blob wire format (capture list in the form header). Medium-large; sensitive-area review. The lazy chain is O(n) by design (decision 31 kept foldl's lazy accumulator; foldl-strict is the constant-space form), so this only removes the extra list retention. Owner decision needed before any work.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: Coordinator: both parts are required together; neither alone fixes it. Flat thunks alone: the accumulator thunk op(i, l head) still needs l, and l is the cons cell that leads to the rest of the list. Selector rule alone: l head becomes the element, but the thunk still captures the whole frame, which holds l. Together the thunk captures only the element, i and op. The wire-format change comes with flat thunks; the selector rule alone needs none. Neither part has been prototyped.

comments.text: Design: root cause is detect_block_params/collect_block_uses (typecheck/check.rs) scanning Let binding values at depth instead of depth+1. A let is recursive, so values sit inside its scope; the list-destructuring desugar (let __p1 = HEAD(__p0) in let x = __p1.x) made the inner __p1.x look like a projection of lambda param 0. Fix: scan let values at depth+1. Narrow (one line); no unify.rs change. Side effects: list-block(5) no longer warns (tuple param is any, previously accidental warning); block params projected inside nested lets now warn on non-blocks (previously missed).

title: Checker: derived monad map on identity-like monads warns 'expected a number, found number'
description: Repro: `id-bind(m, f): f(m)` / `id-monad: monad({bind: id-bind, return: id})` / `x: id-monad.map(inc, 41)`. Also `random.map(inc, random.int(10))` warns "expected a number, found any → {..}". From 119_monad_utility.eu, 120_random_monad.eu. Found by eu-oaz72.168.

title: eu test follow-ups from #1194: duplicate inputs, result-file collisions, -o ignored, multi-dir report location
description: From eu-oaz72.45 (PR #1194, merged 63a8bde) review, non-blocking: (1) overlapping inputs (a.eu a.eu, dir/ dir/a.eu) run and report a file twice; (2) x.eu and x.yaml in one dir overwrite each other's result files (pre-existing); (3) eu test -o is ignored, the report always lands in the first plan's .result dir (pre-existing); (4) the report for inputs across several dirs is written under the first dir only; (5) resolve_input stops at the first -L dir whose canonicalize fails (pre-existing); (6) error_test_with_binary still reads only the last input (only reached from harness_test.rs). design:
Design (src/driver/tester.rs, src/core/analyse/testplan.rs; verdict semantics unchanged):
1. Duplicates: test() first resolves every input to canonical test-file paths (a directory expands to its files), drops any path already seen (first occurrence wins, order kept), then loads one plan per file. `a.eu a.eu` and `dir dir/a.eu` run a.eu once.
2. Result files: evidence/report sidecars are named from the full file name (x.eu.evidence.yaml, x.yaml.report.yaml) instead of replacing the extension, so x.eu and x.yaml in one dir no longer overwrite each other.
3. -o: `eu test -o PATH` writes the HTML report to PATH (cli help: "Output file for test report"); the combined results.yaml stays in the report directory. Test runs never inherit -o.
4. Report directory: unchanged when every test file is in one directory (DIR/.result/RUN/). When they span several, the report goes in the current directory's .result/RUN/ rather than the first input's. Documented in docs/guide/testing.md.
5. resolve_input: a lib dir where the path does not exist is skipped instead of aborting the search, so `eu test -L d x.eu` finds d/x.eu.
6. error_test_with_binary runs every input (each its own error test), exit 1 if any fails; stale doc on error_test fixed.
Tests: tests/test_several_inputs_test.rs drives the binary (CLI-only; no .eu program can reach this), each fault-injection verified.

description: From eu-oaz72.9 (PR #1186) review, non-blocking. comments.author: Claude
comments.text: Design. (1) PipelineResult carries the run's cancel flag; apply_pipeline_result drops results whose flag is set or whose document is no longer open (close and newer edits already set it). (2) Shutdown sets every cancel flag so debouncing runs stop. (3) Decision: failed sends of diagnostics and refresh requests are ignored (logged once per failure to stderr), not fatal. A failed write means the client's reader is gone; LSP clients end a server with shutdown/exit or by closing stdin, and the main loop already ends on either, so dying on a failed best-effort notification only turns a transient/closed client into exit 2 and loses the shutdown handshake. Responses and the loop keep ending on stdin EOF/exit. (4) Document exit codes 0/1/2 for eu lsp in docs/reference/cli.md (2 = server error incl. reader-thread failure). Tidy: respond() decodes params directly (no unreachable MethodMismatch arm); drop the duplicate pipeline_rx clone. Tests in tests/lsp_stdio_test.rs, plus in-process tests where the stale window is not reachable over stdio.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: Design: bound the pipe drain by the deadline rather than kill the process group (portable; the group kill needs unsafe libc on unix and job objects on Windows). Readers stream chunks over an mpsc channel; the caller collects until both reach EOF or the deadline instant passes, then returns what it has (None on timeout, after killing the direct child). A reader blocked on a grandchild-held pipe is left detached. title: Design arbitrary-precision integers (bignum) for eucalypt
description: Owner decision 2026-11-12: roadmap design item. Today numbers are serde_json::Number (i64/u64/f64): + and * error on overflow, ^ will error too (eu-oaz72.12). Modular cases are covered by eu-oaz72.24 (mulmod/powmod/modinv in i128). Remaining need: exact arithmetic beyond 64 bits for linear algebra and rationals on large values (AoC 2023 d24 p2 cross products ~1e29, 2022 d21 p2 solving through divisions), where f64 rounding gives wrong answers. Design questions: automatic promotion on overflow (Python semantics) vs an explicit bigint type; whether to add exact rationals; storage of digits in the GC heap (no Rust Vec/BigInt allocations inside heap objects, per the eu-oaz72.5 rule) or inline small/large split; arithmetic, comparison, hashing/ordering (dict keys, eu-oaz72.21), rendering (YAML/JSON refuse values above i64 today), type checker; performance impact on the common i64 path (must be negligible); replacing serde_json::Number as the core number type.
acceptance_criteria: Design note in docs/superpowers/plans with a recommendation, semantics, storage layout under the GC-heap rule, rendering rules, and a measured plan for zero regression on i64 arithmetic; ROADMAP entry added.

title: (BUG) primary blames the wrong argument of the right call
description:
When a type mismatch occurs inside a callee, the primary label is placed on an argument expression at the call site that did NOT supply the offending value.

SPECIMEN (four-file import chain, see report section 13):

  # lib/geometry.eu
  side-mm(key, shape): (shape lookup(key)) to-mm(shape.units)
  #                     ^col 22 supplies n    ^col 48 supplies unit

  # lib/units.eu
  to-mm(unit, n): n * (factors lookup(unit))

With a string in the data, 0.14 reports:

  error[EU-EVAL-TYPE]: type mismatch: expected number, found string "8"
    ┌─ geometry.eu:3:48
  3 │ side-mm(key, shape): (shape lookup(key)) to-mm(shape.units)
    │                                                ^^^^^

The caret is on 'shape.units', which supplies 'unit' and is perfectly correct. The string arrives via '(shape lookup(key))' at column 22, which supplies 'n'. Right call, wrong argument. 0.13.2 behaves identically, so this is longstanding rather than a 0.14 regression.

WHY IT HAPPENS (hypothesis, needs confirming): 'to-mm(shape.units)' is a juxtaposed call with exactly one explicit argument, and 'n' is supplied by catenation as the receiver. The blame appears to pick the App node's argument expression -- the only explicit one -- rather than the argument that carried the mismatched value.

WHAT CORRECT LOOKS LIKE: blame the argument that supplied the offending value; failing that, blame the parameter inside the callee ('n' at units.eu:4:17) with the caller's expression as a secondary. Anything but an innocent sibling argument.

DIFFICULTY -- do not assume this is cheap. The mismatch is raised inside to-mm's body at the '*', where 'n' is known to be the bad value, but mapping that parameter back to the caller's argument EXPRESSION crosses the call boundary and is not obviously available at raise time. The catenation-supplied receiver makes it harder, since it is not in the arg tuple at all. Scope the investigation before committing to a fix.

DISTINCT FROM eu-1tkk.7.38, which concerns span WIDTH (callee name vs whole call). This is about WHICH argument is blamed, and 7.38's fix does not reach it. Also distinct from eu-1tkk.7.13/.14, which concern value provenance back to the data literal; this defect is present even when provenance is irrelevant.

Evidence: docs/superpowers/reports/2026-08-01-0.14-diagnostics-demonstration.md section 13
notes: 2026-08-07 coordinator: reset from in_progress to open — no active work. Explicitly blocked on eu-1tkk.7.45 (per-argument value provenance): the 7.45 implementation attempt established that only per-argument provenance makes correct argument blame tractable; the sticky-register form does not help. Dependency now recorded so this shows blocked rather than ready. Follows 7.45 to 0.15 (both under sub-epic eu-1tkk.7, parented to epic eu-sks3l).

comments.author: greg
comments.text:
Investigated 2026-08-01 (Clarion, alongside eu-1tkk.7.40). NOT FIXED — left open deliberately.

Two findings that change the framing:

1. The bead's specimen produces NO type warning ('eu check' is silent — the string comes from data, which gradual typing cannot see). So eu-1tkk.7.40 does not unlock it. 7.40 does help the adjacent swapped-parameter case, which the checker does catch.

2. The cause is not argument identity. The blamed Smid is machine.annotation() — a single register holding whichever thunk was forced LAST. Confirmed by deleting the use of 'unit' from the callee: the caret immediately moves off the innocent sibling. The bead's hypothesis (blame picks the App node's only explicit argument) is not what happens.

Mechanism: BcContinuation::Branch/BranchPredecoded capture 'annotation: state.annotation' when a case is pushed and never restore it on return; SeqBind and ApplyTo both do. Same omission in vm.rs, which is why 0.13.2 matches.

The obvious fix was implemented and measured against the 214-fixture corpus: 7 fixtures moved, 3 better (080/082 array cases stop blaming arr.from-flat; the 7.39 specimen is fixed), 2 clearly worse (provocations/metadata_span blames the callee's definition instead of the line holding the mistake; errors/149_not_value_source_loc degrades to a six-line whole-file caret), 2 marginal. Reverted.

Same mechanism, seen twice: when the last-forced thunk IS the offending value, stale blame is excellent; when it is an innocent sibling, it is terrible. Restoring the case site does not win that lottery, it just biases blame inward. What is actually needed is value provenance — eu-1tkk.7.13/.14 — despite this bead distinguishing itself from those.

Evidence: docs/superpowers/reports/2026-08-01-eu-1tkk-7-39-7-40-argument-blame.md (PR #1105).

title: [bug] stg::syntax::ex test-fixture combinators do not match their names
description:
Found during the eu-frf2o sibling-group audit.

src/eval/stg/syntax.rs's 'pub mod ex' (#[cfg(test)], documented as 'Example STG expression for use in tests') appears to be entirely unreferenced, and two of its combinators do not compute what they are named:

  ex::s()  = lambda(3, let_([value(app(lref(1),[lref(2)])),   // g(x)
                             value(app(lref(0),[lref(2)]))],  // f(x)
                            app(lref(0), [lref(1)])))

The let body names binding 0 applied to binding 1, i.e. g(x)(f(x)). The S combinator is f(x)(g(x)) — the operands are swapped.

  ex::compose() = lambda(2, let_([lambda(1, app(lref(2),[lref(0)]))],
                                  app(lref(1), [lref(0)])))

With arity 2 there is no x in scope, so the binding is the function (\\x. g(x)) and the body applies f to that function: f(\\x.g(x)), not \\x. f(g(x)). The inline comment '// [gx] [f g]' suggests the author believed the binding was g(x).

No runtime reach — the module is test-only and unused — so this is housekeeping, not a defect in the language. Either fix the two fixtures or delete the module if nothing needs it.

The let/letrec structure of both is correct (bindings reference the enclosing frame, body references the group); only the operand wiring is wrong.
